script.opening: "Doc, I’ll be honest, I nearly didn’t book this — I’ve been putting it off for weeks. I’m just not sleeping — awake at four every morning, head going. And I’ve been short with everyone. I don’t need to be sat here talking about feelings; I just need something to knock me out at night so I can function on the farm. I’m not one of these depression types."

facts.text: If explored: low mood most days for months, lost interest in things he loved, 6 kg weight loss, early-morning waking, poor concentration, feels he’s "failed" — a clear depressive picture he resists labelling. Stoical "farmers don’t get depressed" framing.

On sensitive direct questioning: he has had thoughts that "everyone’d be better off without me" and, if asked carefully, has thought about using his shotgun — he has access to firearms at home. This is high lethal-means access plus hopelessness: serious suicide risk requiring explicit assessment, not assumption.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "just give me sleeping tablets" is partly a wish to avoid the truth, and partly that he has genuinely contemplated ending things and is testing whether anyone will notice. The triggers he hasn’t volunteered: the farm is failing financially (possible repossession) and his wife has just left. He feels shame as "the man who couldn’t hold it together".

Strong male/occupational stigma ("not one of these depression types"), rural isolation, and a culture of not asking for help — farmers are a known high-suicide-risk group. The reluctance is the danger.

Officially: sleeping tablets to keep functioning. What is needed: explicit suicide-risk assessment, recognition of depression, safety planning including lethal-means (firearms) safety — the guns and ammunition leaving his control today (a registered firearms dealer, another certificate holder or the police), not just locked away — treatment, and — if risk warrants — awareness of the duty to consider informing the firearms licensing authority. All delivered without shaming him into silence.

ice.ideas: It’s just insomnia and stress from the farm; he needs sleeping tablets, not "feelings talk"; he’s "not the depression type".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a failing farm (possible repossession) and his wife leaving, deep shame as a man who "couldn’t hold it together", and genuine thoughts of ending his life using his shotgun, which he’s testing whether anyone will notice.
ice.expectations: A prescription for sleeping tablets. What he actually needs: an explicit risk assessment, depression treatment, lethal-means safety planning (the guns out of his control today), and compassionate handling of stigma.

cues: "Just knock me out so I can function" + early waking + snappy — a depressive picture he’s reframing as mere insomnia.
"Everyone’d be better off" if it surfaces — explicit suicidal ideation; ask directly about plan, means and the firearms.
Stoical "not the depression type", a farmer, isolated — high-risk demographic; the reluctance itself is the warning.

checkpoints.text: Recognises DEPRESSION behind the "insomnia" (pervasive low mood, anhedonia, weight loss, early waking, hopelessness) rather than simply prescribing a hypnotic, and does not collude with the "just stress / not the depression type" framing

Conducts an EXPLICIT suicide-risk assessment: asks directly about thoughts of being better off dead, suicidal ideation, plan, intent, means and preparatory acts — and specifically about ACCESS TO FIREARMS at home — plus protective factors; recognises asking does not increase risk

Addresses LETHAL-MEANS SAFETY: negotiates the guns and ammunition leaving his control today — held by a registered firearms dealer or another certificate holder, or surrendered to the police — as a core part of safety planning for a high-risk patient with firearm access; recognises that "secure storage" in a cabinet he holds the key to does NOT remove access

Knows the FIREARMS DUTY: if there is a genuine risk to safety, a GP may need to consider informing the police/firearms licensing department — a justified breach of confidentiality in the public interest (GMC Confidentiality 2017: disclosure may be justified to inform decisions about fitness to hold a firearm or shotgun certificate where not disclosing may expose him or others to a risk of death or serious harm; Home Office statutory guidance on firearms licensing, in force from November 2021) — with suicidal thoughts and a plan involving his shotgun, this threshold is met; ideally discussed with the patient first and done proportionately

Initiates appropriate management: depression treatment (NICE NG222: for more severe depression, individual CBT combined with an antidepressant is a first-line option; with suicide risk, review within 1 week of starting and consider toxicity in overdose and limited quantities), same-day crisis team assessment because his plan involves a firearm, bloods for the 6 kg weight loss, treats the alcohol as a contributor, and surfaces the social drivers (farm finances, separation) signposting practical support (e.g. farming charities)

Overcomes the stigma with warmth and normalisation so he engages: validates the strain, reframes depression as an illness not a weakness, and creates safety to disclose rather than shaming him into silence
Handles the firearms/confidentiality conversation honestly and respectfully — explaining any need to act on risk WITH him wherever possible, preserving the relationship

Safety-nets robustly and documents: crisis routes (999/A&E, NHS 111 mental health option, Samaritans 116 123) if thoughts intensify, someone with him tonight, a safety plan including the guns leaving his control, a call the next day and review within 1 week, no driving until reviewed (DVLA), who to contact, and coordinated treatment — a concrete plan, not a hypnotic and a goodbye

worked.txt: "I’ll happily help with the sleep — but waking at four with your head racing, going off your food, snapping at everyone, losing interest in things: that’s not just bad sleep, that’s often what low mood looks like in men, especially men who’d never use the word ‘depression’. There’s no weakness in it; it’s an illness, and it’s treatable. Can we look at the whole picture, not just the nights?"

"I’m going to ask you something directly, because I ask anyone who’s this low and it matters. When things have felt this heavy, have you had thoughts that you’d be better off not here, or that others would be better off without you? … Thank you for being honest. Have you thought about how? … And you’ve got the guns at home, haven’t you."

"Here’s where I have to be straight with you, man to man, because I’d rather have an awkward conversation than the alternative. With thoughts like that and the shotguns in the house, I want those guns out of the house today — held by your dealer or another certificate holder, or handed in to the police. Locking them in the cabinet isn’t enough while you’ve still got the key and feel like this. Not forever necessarily; just while we get you through this. Would you work with me on that?"

"And I won’t hide this from you: because of what you’ve told me about the gun, I do need to let the police firearms licensing team know — the doctors’ confidentiality guidance from the GMC supports that when someone who holds a gun certificate is at risk. I’d always rather do that WITH you, in the open, than behind your back. But your life matters more to me than the certificate, and I think it does to you too, even on the hard mornings."

"Can I ask what’s been crushing you? … The farm, and her leaving. Alan, that’s an enormous amount — your livelihood and your marriage at once, and a lifetime of being the one who copes. No wonder. None of this makes you a failure; it makes you a man carrying far too much alone. There’s real help — for the head, and for the farm side too; there are people for exactly this."

"So: let’s treat the depression properly — I’d suggest starting a medication and getting you some talking support, and easing off the drink, which is making it worse. The guns leave the house today, and I’m asking the crisis team to see you today too. Please don’t drive until you’re feeling better. Is there someone who can be with you tonight? If those thoughts get stronger, or you feel you might act, call 999 or go to A&E; NHS 111 with the mental health option or Samaritans on 116 123 are there any hour. I’ll ring you tomorrow and see you within a week, not weeks. You came in for sleeping tablets; what you’re leaving with is people who aren’t going to let you go under."

f.learning: "Just insomnia" in a stoical, isolated man is frequently depression — and farmers/men with firearms access are a recognised high-suicide-risk group, so the reluctance itself is the warning. The non-negotiable task is an EXPLICIT suicide-risk assessment (thoughts of being better off dead, ideation, plan, intent, means, preparatory acts) including direct enquiry about FIREARM ACCESS — asking does not increase risk. With high lethal-means access plus hopelessness, lethal-means safety (the guns and ammunition leaving his control today — a registered firearms dealer, another certificate holder or the police; a cabinet he holds the key to is not enough) is central to the safety plan, and the GP must know the firearms duty: a genuine safety risk can justify informing the police/firearms licensing department in the public interest (GMC Confidentiality 2017; Home Office statutory guidance on firearms licensing), done proportionately and, wherever possible, with the patient. Treat the depression per NICE NG222 (CBT with an antidepressant for more severe depression; review within 1 week when there is suicide risk), with same-day crisis team assessment for a plan involving a firearm. The examinable hidden agenda is shame-laden (a failing farm and a marriage ending) and a man testing whether anyone notices his despair. Overcome stigma with warmth so he engages, treat the depression and alcohol, surface the social drivers and signpost practical help, handle the confidentiality/firearms conversation honestly, and safety-net with crisis routes and early follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025) · NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · GMC Confidentiality (2017) · Home Office Statutory guidance for chief officers of police on firearms licensing (2021, revised) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
knowledge.summary: Early waking, weight loss, loss of interest and hopelessness in a stoical farmer is depression, not insomnia. Ask directly about suicide and the guns, make the firearms safe, involve the crisis team when there is a plan, and know when to inform the police firearms licensing team.

points.t: Low mood, anhedonia, early-morning waking, 6 kg weight loss, poor concentration and feeling a failure over months is a depressive episode. Men often present with sleep, irritability or drinking. Do not prescribe a hypnotic and miss it.

Ask about feeling better off dead, thoughts of suicide, plans, means, preparations and what keeps him going. Asking does not increase risk. NICE NG225 advises against risk scales or low/medium/high labels to decide care; the plan follows the whole picture.

Access to firearms with suicidal thoughts and hopelessness is a serious risk. Agree today that the guns and ammunition leave his control: held by a registered firearms dealer or another certificate holder, or surrendered to the police. A locked cabinet he holds the key to is not enough.

GMC Confidentiality (2017): disclosure to the police may be justified in the public interest to inform decisions about fitness to hold a firearm or shotgun certificate, if not disclosing may expose the patient or others to a risk of death or serious harm. Tell him first and involve him where you can; document the reasons.

NICE NG222: for more severe depression, a combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant is a first-line option. When there is a risk of suicide, review within 1 week of starting an antidepressant and consider toxicity in overdose and limiting quantities. A plan involving firearms needs same-day crisis team assessment.
Quantify drinking (AUDIT-C); alcohol worsens mood, sleep and impulsivity. With 6 kg weight loss, check bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, HbA1c) to rule out a physical cause.
DVLA: depression with significant memory or concentration problems, agitation, behavioural disturbance or suicidal thoughts must be notified, and he should not drive until assessed.

dg.d: Accepted “it’s just sleep” as a start and explored what keeps him awake.
The failing farm, his wife leaving, alcohol, isolation, and male and farming stigma.
Bloods for weight loss (FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, HbA1c); AUDIT-C; PHQ-9 to track severity.
Depressive episode versus primary insomnia, alcohol-related low mood, or a physical cause of weight loss.
Explicit suicide questions: ideation, plan, means (firearms), preparation, protective factors.
Names depression with suicidal thoughts and a firearms plan, in plain language.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Guns out of his control today; same-day crisis team; CBT plus antidepressant; no hypnotic alone; firearms licensing informed with him.
Alcohol reduction, farming financial support, relationship loss, driving advice.
Call tomorrow, review within a week, 999/A&E, NHS 111 mental health option, Samaritans, company tonight.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the pause after “everything, really”, the drinking and “I’ve failed”.
Idea (just insomnia); concern (shame, the farm, the marriage, thoughts of dying); expectation (sleeping tablets).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — a failing farm (possible repossession) and his wife leaving, deep shame as a man who "couldn’t hold it together", and genuine thoughts of ending his life using his shotgun, which he’s testing whether anyone will notice — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Foister, I’m Dr Lee. Can you hear and see me all right, and are you somewhere private? Tell me what’s been going on with the sleep.
model.why: Checks the video set-up and privacy, then opens the floor

model.text: I’m just not sleeping. Awake at four every morning, head going. I’ve been short with everyone. I don’t need to talk about feelings, I just need something to knock me out so I can function on the farm. I’m not one of these depression types.
Fair enough, and I will help with the sleep. To do that properly I need to understand what’s keeping you awake. Can I ask some questions, and then we’ll agree a plan?
model.why: Accepts his agenda while widening it

model.text: Go on then.
When you wake at four, what goes through your head?
model.why: Open question into the content of the insomnia

model.text: The farm. Money. It’s not doing well. (Pause.) Everything, really.
How has your mood been over the last few months? Do you still enjoy the things you used to?
Can’t remember the last time I enjoyed anything. I’ve lost weight, about a stone. Can’t concentrate. Feel like I’ve failed.
And how much are you drinking at the moment?
More than I should. A few drinks most nights to get off to sleep.
You mentioned the farm. Has anything else changed at home?
model.why: Follows the cue towards the social drivers

model.text: (Long pause.) My wife’s left. A few weeks ago.
I’m sorry. Your livelihood and your marriage at the same time is a huge amount for anyone to carry.
model.why: Acknowledges the losses before moving to risk

model.text: I ask this of anyone carrying this much, and I’d like an honest answer. Have you had thoughts that you’d be better off dead, or that others would be better off without you?
(Looks away.) Sometimes. Everyone’d be better off without me.
Thank you for telling me. Have you thought about how you might do it?
I’ve got the shotgun. I’ve thought about using it.
Have you done anything to prepare, like writing notes, or taking the gun out with that in mind? And what has stopped you so far?
No. Nothing like that. I just think about it, mostly at night.

Alan, what you’re describing isn’t weakness, and it isn’t just bad sleep. It’s depression, an illness that is treatable. And right now it’s telling you things about yourself that aren’t true. I’m worried about your safety, and I want to act on that today.
model.why: Names depression and the level of concern plainly

model.text: I didn’t want to make a fuss.
The most important thing is the guns. Would you agree to them leaving the house today, held by your dealer or another certificate holder, or handed in to the police, until you’re well?
I need them for the farm. But… yes. All right.

Thank you. I also need to be open with you. Because of the risk, I will let the police firearms licensing team know. I’d much rather do that with you than behind your back. It’s about keeping you alive, not punishing you.
model.why: Explains the justified disclosure honestly and with him

model.text: I’m going to ask the crisis team to see you today. Then we treat the depression properly: talking therapy and an antidepressant work best together for how low you are. No sleeping tablets on their own, and let’s cut the drinking right back, because it’s making the mood and the nights worse.
model.why: Same-day crisis referral and NG222 treatment; addresses alcohol

model.text: The crisis team. Today?

Today. And there are farming charities that help with exactly the money side, so you don’t carry that alone either. I’ll arrange some bloods too because of the weight loss. Please don’t drive until you’re feeling better.
model.why: Addresses social drivers, physical causes and driving

model.text: Is there someone who can be with you tonight? If the thoughts get stronger, call 999 or go to A&E. For support any time, NHS 111 with the mental health option, or Samaritans on 116 123. I’ll ring you tomorrow and see you within a week.
model.why: Crisis routes, company tonight and early follow-up

model.text: I’ll ring someone.
Before we finish, can you tell me what’s happening with the guns today and what you’ll do if the thoughts come back tonight?
Guns go to the dealer this afternoon. Crisis team will call. If it gets bad, 999.
That’s right. You came in for sleeping tablets and you’ve told me something much harder. That took courage. Anything else you want to ask?
model.why: Validates disclosure and shares the floor

model.text: No. Thanks, doc.

social.t: Financial pressure on the farm, long solitary hours and a culture of coping alone. Farming charities (for example the Farming Community Network and RABI) help with money worries and practical support.
His wife leaving removes his main support. Ask who can be with him and who he trusts.

legal.t: Home Office statutory guidance (in force from November 2021) gives GPs a role in firearms licensing. GMC Confidentiality (2017) supports disclosure to the police where a certificate holder may pose a risk of death or serious harm. Tell him, involve him, and document the reasons.
DVLA: depression with suicidal thoughts, significant concentration problems or agitation must be notified. Advise him not to drive, including farm vehicles on the road, until reviewed.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): where possible, tell the patient before disclosing and seek his agreement. A covert disclosure damages trust when he most needs it.
Record the direct risk questions and answers, the firearms plan, the disclosure and its justification, the crisis referral and the follow-up date.

community.t: 999 or A&E if at immediate risk; NHS 111 mental health option (24/7); Samaritans 116 123; local crisis team.

Hopelessness and recent losses; ask about any preparation
Heavy drinking, isolation, and a high-risk occupational group

Alcohol each night; stigma about mental health in farming
ice: Idea: it’s just insomnia and stress; he is “not the depression type”

playbook.diagnosis: “This isn’t just poor sleep. You have depression, it’s an illness, and it’s treatable. The thoughts about the gun worry me, and I want to act on them today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Depression is like a heavy fog that changes how everything looks: the farm, your worth, the future. It isn’t a weakness. With the right treatment the fog lifts, and things look different again.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in for sleep because that felt like the acceptable thing to ask for. What you’ve told me is much harder, and I’m glad you did.”
management.psychosocial: Farming charity support for the finances, someone with him tonight, alcohol reduction, and a plan he agrees to for the guns.
sharedPlan: Firearms out of his control today; police firearms licensing informed, with him
Same-day crisis team assessment; then CBT plus an antidepressant (NICE NG222)
No hypnotic alone; reduce alcohol; bloods for weight loss; no driving for now
safetyNet: 999 or A&E if thoughts intensify; NHS 111 mental health option; Samaritans 116 123
GP call tomorrow and review within 1 week

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you can see depression and suicide risk behind a request for sleeping tablets, and whether you act on firearm access. Most failing candidates never ask about the guns.

items.fail: Prescribing a hypnotic and sleep hygiene advice for “insomnia”.
items.why: “Did not recognise the underlying problem.” Early waking, weight loss and anhedonia are depression.
items.fix: Ask what he thinks about at 4am, then screen mood, enjoyment, weight and concentration.

items.fail: Never asking about suicide because he seems stoical and in control.
items.why: “Risk not assessed.” Stoicism is part of the danger in this group.
items.fix: “Have you had thoughts you’d be better off dead? Have you thought about how?”

items.fail: Hearing about the shotgun and moving on without a plan for it.
items.why: Access to lethal means is the most changeable part of the risk.
items.fix: Negotiate the guns leaving his control today and inform firearms licensing.

items.fail: Informing the police without telling him, or threatening it to get compliance.
items.why: “Did not involve the patient in decisions.” It breaks trust at the worst moment.
items.fix: “I’d rather do this with you than behind your back. It’s about keeping you alive.”

items.fail: “So, are you depressed?” to a man who has just said he’s not the type.
items.why: Labels he rejects close the conversation. Examiners note the lack of rapport.
items.fix: Start with his words (sleep, temper, the farm), then name depression as an illness once he has told you more.

items.fail: Routine review in four weeks with a list of numbers.
items.why: “Follow-up not appropriate to the level of risk.”
items.fix: Same-day crisis team, call tomorrow, review within a week, company tonight, and teach-back.

wordPics.pass: Recognises depression; asks directly about suicide and access to firearms; arranges for the guns to be removed; refers to the crisis team; knows the firearms disclosure duty; gives crisis numbers.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: engages a stoical man by accepting his frame first; uncovers the farm and the separation; negotiates the guns leaving the house today; explains the disclosure to firearms licensing honestly and with him; addresses alcohol, finances and driving; calls the next day; checks the safety plan with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “I can give you a short course of sleeping tablets to tide you over.”
avoid.instead: “Waking at four with your mind racing is often low mood. Let’s treat what’s causing it.”
avoid.why: A hypnotic misses the depression and gives a means of overdose.

avoid.dont: “You’re not thinking of doing anything silly, are you?”
avoid.instead: “Have you had thoughts that you’d be better off dead? Have you thought about how?”
avoid.why: A leading, minimising question invites “no”. Direct questions get honest answers.

SCA_STEM.name: Alan Foister
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
Holds a shotgun and firearm certificate (occupational, farmer)
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation about poor sleep and being “short with everyone”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025) · NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · GMC Confidentiality (2017) · Home Office Statutory guidance for chief officers of police on firearms licensing (2021, revised) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Early waking, weight loss, loss of interest and hopelessness in a stoical farmer is depression, not insomnia. Ask directly about suicide and the guns, make the firearms safe, involve the crisis team when there is a plan, and know when to inform the police firearms licensing team.

points.t: Low mood, anhedonia, early-morning waking, 6 kg weight loss, poor concentration and feeling a failure over months is a depressive episode. Men often present with sleep, irritability or drinking. Do not prescribe a hypnotic and miss it.

Ask about feeling better off dead, thoughts of suicide, plans, means, preparations and what keeps him going. Asking does not increase risk. NICE NG225 advises against risk scales or low/medium/high labels to decide care; the plan follows the whole picture.

Access to firearms with suicidal thoughts and hopelessness is a serious risk. Agree today that the guns and ammunition leave his control: held by a registered firearms dealer or another certificate holder, or surrendered to the police. A locked cabinet he holds the key to is not enough.

GMC Confidentiality (2017): disclosure to the police may be justified in the public interest to inform decisions about fitness to hold a firearm or shotgun certificate, if not disclosing may expose the patient or others to a risk of death or serious harm. Tell him first and involve him where you can; document the reasons.

NICE NG222: for more severe depression, a combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant is a first-line option. When there is a risk of suicide, review within 1 week of starting an antidepressant and consider toxicity in overdose and limiting quantities. A plan involving firearms needs same-day crisis team assessment.
Quantify drinking (AUDIT-C); alcohol worsens mood, sleep and impulsivity. With 6 kg weight loss, check bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, HbA1c) to rule out a physical cause.
DVLA: depression with significant memory or concentration problems, agitation, behavioural disturbance or suicidal thoughts must be notified, and he should not drive until assessed.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Accepted “it’s just sleep” as a start and explored what keeps him awake.
The failing farm, his wife leaving, alcohol, isolation, and male and farming stigma.
Picked up the pause after “everything, really”, the drinking and “I’ve failed”.
Idea (just insomnia); concern (shame, the farm, the marriage, thoughts of dying); expectation (sleeping tablets).
Bloods for weight loss (FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, HbA1c); AUDIT-C; PHQ-9 to track severity.
Depressive episode versus primary insomnia, alcohol-related low mood, or a physical cause of weight loss.
Explicit suicide questions: ideation, plan, means (firearms), preparation, protective factors.
Names depression with suicidal thoughts and a firearms plan, in plain language.
Guns out of his control today; same-day crisis team; CBT plus antidepressant; no hypnotic alone; firearms licensing informed with him.
Alcohol reduction, farming financial support, relationship loss, driving advice.
Call tomorrow, review within a week, 999/A&E, NHS 111 mental health option, Samaritans, company tonight.

social.t: Financial pressure on the farm, long solitary hours and a culture of coping alone. Farming charities (for example the Farming Community Network and RABI) help with money worries and practical support.
His wife leaving removes his main support. Ask who can be with him and who he trusts.

legal.t: Home Office statutory guidance (in force from November 2021) gives GPs a role in firearms licensing. GMC Confidentiality (2017) supports disclosure to the police where a certificate holder may pose a risk of death or serious harm. Tell him, involve him, and document the reasons.
DVLA: depression with suicidal thoughts, significant concentration problems or agitation must be notified. Advise him not to drive, including farm vehicles on the road, until reviewed.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): where possible, tell the patient before disclosing and seek his agreement. A covert disclosure damages trust when he most needs it.
Record the direct risk questions and answers, the firearms plan, the disclosure and its justification, the crisis referral and the follow-up date.

community.t: 999 or A&E if at immediate risk; NHS 111 mental health option (24/7); Samaritans 116 123; local crisis team.

redFlags: Thoughts of being better off dead with a plan involving his shotgun
Hopelessness and recent losses; ask about any preparation
Heavy drinking, isolation, and a high-risk occupational group
psychosocial: Wife recently left; who is around him now
Alcohol each night; stigma about mental health in farming
ice: Idea: it’s just insomnia and stress; he is “not the depression type”
Concern: shame at not coping, the farm, the marriage, and thoughts of ending his life
Expectation: something to knock him out at night

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This isn’t just poor sleep. You have depression, it’s an illness, and it’s treatable. The thoughts about the gun worry me, and I want to act on them today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Depression is like a heavy fog that changes how everything looks: the farm, your worth, the future. It isn’t a weakness. With the right treatment the fog lifts, and things look different again.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in for sleep because that felt like the acceptable thing to ask for. What you’ve told me is much harder, and I’m glad you did.”
management.psychosocial: Farming charity support for the finances, someone with him tonight, alcohol reduction, and a plan he agrees to for the guns.
sharedPlan: Firearms out of his control today; police firearms licensing informed, with him
Same-day crisis team assessment; then CBT plus an antidepressant (NICE NG222)
No hypnotic alone; reduce alcohol; bloods for weight loss; no driving for now

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you can see depression and suicide risk behind a request for sleeping tablets, and whether you act on firearm access. Most failing candidates never ask about the guns.

items.fail: Prescribing a hypnotic and sleep hygiene advice for “insomnia”.
items.why: “Did not recognise the underlying problem.” Early waking, weight loss and anhedonia are depression.
items.fix: Ask what he thinks about at 4am, then screen mood, enjoyment, weight and concentration.

items.fail: Never asking about suicide because he seems stoical and in control.
items.why: “Risk not assessed.” Stoicism is part of the danger in this group.
items.fix: “Have you had thoughts you’d be better off dead? Have you thought about how?”

items.fail: Hearing about the shotgun and moving on without a plan for it.
items.why: Access to lethal means is the most changeable part of the risk.
items.fix: Negotiate the guns leaving his control today and inform firearms licensing.

items.fail: Informing the police without telling him, or threatening it to get compliance.
items.why: “Did not involve the patient in decisions.” It breaks trust at the worst moment.
items.fix: “I’d rather do this with you than behind your back. It’s about keeping you alive.”

items.fail: “So, are you depressed?” to a man who has just said he’s not the type.
items.why: Labels he rejects close the conversation. Examiners note the lack of rapport.
items.fix: Start with his words (sleep, temper, the farm), then name depression as an illness once he has told you more.

items.fail: Routine review in four weeks with a list of numbers.
items.why: “Follow-up not appropriate to the level of risk.”
items.fix: Same-day crisis team, call tomorrow, review within a week, company tonight, and teach-back.
